items.prompt: Define a directed response, and state what it is not.
items.canonical_answer: A directed response is a new text written from a source for a form, audience and purpose the task sets, re-using the source’s content in a new style. It is not a summary of the source and not a copy of its wording: the content is carried across, and everything else — register, voice, structure — is built for the new reader the task names.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: a new text from a source, for a set form, audience and purpose, re-using its content.
The boundaries — not a summary, not a copy — are part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: State the two steps of reshaping a source.
items.canonical_answer: First select: from everything the source contains, keep the content the new purpose needs and leave the rest. Then change: register, voice and structure go over to the new form, and the content arrives in your own words. The order matters, because selecting first means every sentence is written for the new reader rather than translated from the old one.
marking_guidance: Credit the two steps in order: select, then change.
The order is the point: an answer that translates sentence by sentence has reversed it.

objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: What is the difference between re-using a source’s content and lifting its wording, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: Re-using content keeps what the source says — facts, viewpoint, people — in your own words; lifting copies phrases or sentences across, which is copying rather than re-use. The test is the sentence’s authorship: could the source’s writer have written it? If yes, it is theirs, and the response has changed clothing without changing voice — the one thing reshaping must do.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: content carried in new words against wording copied across.
Must give the test: whether the source’s writer could have written the sentence.

objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: This extract is from a source about a library campaign: "The council announced on Tuesday that the library will remain open, with reduced hours, after a petition gathered 4,000 signatures. Volunteers will staff the weekend counter." Rewrite it as the opening of an email to a friend who signed the petition, keeping the content.
items.canonical_answer: Guess what — it worked! The council said on Tuesday the library stays open, though the hours are cut, and that was after all those signatures (4,000 of them — including yours). The weekends will be run by volunteers, so no more Saturday staff, but the doors stay open. I know you signed, so this one is partly yours. (Any rewrite keeps the three facts — the announcement, the reduced hours, the petition’s size and the volunteers — inside an email’s conventions, in an informal register the friend has earned.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the extract’s content carried across, because the words show the re-use.
Credit the fit to the form: an email’s greeting and register, so the change of style shows in the words.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: This extract is from a source about a library campaign: "The council announced on Tuesday that the library will remain open, with reduced hours, after a petition gathered 4,000 signatures. Volunteers will staff the weekend counter." Rewrite it as the opening of a formal public notice, keeping the content.
items.canonical_answer: PUBLIC NOTICE — LIBRARY SERVICE UPDATE. Following Tuesday’s council decision, the library will remain open under revised operating hours. The decision follows a petition of 4,000 signatures. Weekend counter services will in future be staffed by volunteers. Full hours are displayed at the entrance. (The rewrite keeps the three facts and gives them the notice’s register: impersonal, nominalised, and addressed to the public as a body.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the extract’s content carried across into the notice’s words.
Credit the register change: impersonal and formal, because the words show the notice doing its public work.

items.prompt: A directed response begins: "The article tells us that the scheme, ‘a beacon of community spirit’, has ‘transformed the lives of thousands’." What is the learner doing, and what is the cure?
items.canonical_answer: The error is lifting: two of the source’s phrases travel into the response inside quotation marks, which is copying rather than re-use — the words show the source’s voice, not the new text’s. The cure is to write every sentence afresh for the new reader: the beacon of community spirit becomes, for the new audience, whatever the new voice would actually call it — "the whole street turned up", for a friend; "strong local participation", for an official — so the content crosses and the wording does not.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the source’s phrases copied into the response.
Must give the cure: each sentence written afresh for the new reader, because the words show whose voice is speaking.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: A learner’s directed response retells the source from start to finish in the source’s order, at half its length. What has gone wrong, and what does the task actually ask for?
items.canonical_answer: The error is summarising: retelling the source in its own order produces a shorter source, not a new text, because selection and reshaping never happened. The task asks for a new form for a named audience and purpose — which means choosing the content that purpose needs (and dropping the rest), then rebuilding it in the register and structure of the new form. A summary keeps everything in its place; a response keeps the right things in new places.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: a summary in the source’s order instead of a reshaped text.
Must state what the task asks for: selection for the new purpose, and rebuilding for the new form and audience.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: A response to a source about a rescued swimmer adds a detail the source never mentions: that the swimmer had ignored warning signs earlier that day. Why does the addition matter, and what is the rule?
items.canonical_answer: The addition matters because it drifts the response into a different story: the source’s rescue becomes a tale about recklessness, and the new fact carries a judgement the source never made. The rule is that every fact in a directed response traces back to the source — the response re-uses what is there, and invents nothing, because the reader’s trust in the whole answer rests on the two texts telling one story.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the addition changes the story the source tells.
Must give the rule: every fact in the response traces back to the source, so nothing is invented.

objective_titles: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style, in your own words

items.prompt: What does writing in the style of a text mean?
items.canonical_answer: It means taking on the text’s register, its sentence patterns, its voice and its signature features, so a continuation reads as if the same writer wrote it. The style is not one of these things alone: a continuation with the right words in the wrong sentence shapes sounds like someone doing an impression, which is why the four are held together.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: register, sentence patterns, voice and signature features, all taken on.
An answer about copying the topic has confused style with content.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write in the manner of a given text: its register, voice and characteristic features

items.prompt: Give the steps for matching a text’s style.
items.canonical_answer: First name its register: formal, conversational, urgent? Then its typical sentence: long and subordinated, or short and clipped? Then its voice: ironic, confiding, measured? Then two signature features: the aside in dashes, the rule-of-three close, the direct address. Then write with all of them held in mind at once — the continuation is judged by how many of the four it carries, and by how few of its own habits it lets in.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: register, typical sentence, voice, two signature features, then write.
The last step — writing with them held together — is the one that makes the rest worth doing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write in the manner of a given text: its register, voice and characteristic features

items.prompt: Here is an extract, written for the purpose: "The instructions for assembling this desk are, I can now report, a work of fiction. The diagram shows a calm person with two hands. I have four hands’ worth of questions." Continue it for two sentences in the same style.
items.canonical_answer: A continuation in the same style would run: "Step four, for instance, mentions a dowel that appears nowhere in the parts list, and step five mentions it twice. I have written to the manufacturer, in the manner of a person who no longer expects to sleep tonight." (Any two sentences that keep the register, the first-person exasperated voice, the long sentence with a dry aside, and one signature feature such as the deadpan arithmetic are a match.)
marking_guidance: Credit the continuation: two sentences in the extract’s text, because the fit is the skill tested.
Credit the style held in the words: the dry aside, the first person, the register — so the continuation shows the match.

objective_titles: Write in the manner of a given text: its register, voice and characteristic features

items.prompt: List the five things decoded from a directed-response task before writing.
items.canonical_answer: The role: who am I? The form: what kind of text? The audience: who reads it? The purpose: what must it do? And the source content: which facts and viewpoints must come across? Five answers, written down, and every sentence of the response is then checked against them.
marking_guidance: Credit the five in order: role, form, audience, purpose, source content.
The sequence is a decode, so an answer with four of the five has a response built on a missing premise.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write a short piece directed by a text and a task: the role, audience and purpose it sets

items.prompt: Why does the role a task sets matter so much to the writing?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that the role decides the voice and the point of view, and both are in every sentence: a head learner writes with authority and accountability, a visitor with curiosity and gratitude, and a shopkeeper with the detail of the counter. Writing as the role means staying inside that voice — its knowledge, its stakes, its loyalties — which is why writing about the role, as a reporter would, produces sentences no actual head learner would say.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: the role fixes the voice and point of view of every sentence.
An answer that says roles matter because the task says so has not explained the why.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write a short piece directed by a text and a task: the role, audience and purpose it sets

items.prompt: What is the difference between writing as a role and writing about it, and how does the difference show in the sentences?
items.canonical_answer: Writing as the role stays inside its voice: "I have watched this town change for thirty years" is a resident speaking. Writing about the role steps outside: "The residents of the town have watched it change" is a reporter describing. The difference shows in the pronouns, in what the sentence can know (an insider’s memory against a survey’s fact), and in the address — the insider can say "we", the outsider cannot, and the task’s role decides which sentence is available.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: inside the voice against outside it.
Must say how it shows: pronouns, what the sentence can know, the address — so the difference is visible in the words.

items.prompt: What does a 150–200-word directed response contain, and how are the words shared?
items.canonical_answer: It contains the form’s key conventions, the source’s relevant content and a register fitted to the reader. The words are shared across an opening that establishes the form and voice, a body that carries the content in two or three developed moves, and a close that lands the purpose — roughly forty, a hundred and forty, twenty. The range is part of the task: the task sets 150–200 words from an unseen source of about 550–750, and the response’s fit to its length is part of its fit to the form.
marking_guidance: Credit the features: form’s conventions, relevant content, fitted register — the response contains all three.
Credit the sharing: opening, body, close, because the words are budgeted, not poured.

objective_titles: Write 150–200 words whose vocabulary, style and structure fit the form, purpose and audience set

items.prompt: Give a plan for sharing 150–200 words across a directed response.
items.canonical_answer: First, the opening: about thirty to forty words, establishing the form’s convention and the role’s voice. Then the body: about a hundred to a hundred and twenty, carrying the source’s content in two or three developed moves — each one a fact plus its meaning for the new reader. Then the close: about twenty, landing the purpose — the ask, the verdict, the sign-off. Three sections, budgeted before writing, so the length is used rather than reached.
marking_guidance: Credit the three sections with their word shares, in the order: opening, body, close.
The budget is a plan, so an answer that says "write and see" has not planned.

objective_titles: Write 150–200 words whose vocabulary, style and structure fit the form, purpose and audience set

items.prompt: A task sets a speech to a school assembly from a source about a sponsored walk. Opening A: "This walk raised a lot of money which will help the school and the charity, and I would like to tell you about it." Opening B: "Good morning, assembly. Eleven kilometres. Thirty-one of you. One very proud teacher. Let me tell you what Saturday did." Which better fits the form and audience, and what is the case against the other?
items.canonical_answer: B fits better: it carries the speech’s convention (a greeting to the hall), the tricolon of figures, and the speaker’s evident role and pride, and the short sentences suit a listening audience that must be caught at once. The case against A is that it neither addresses the hall nor carries a voice — it could open a report as easily as a speech, so the form is unannounced and the audience unmet. However, A does state its purpose plainly, which is its one virtue; B does that too, in its last sentence.
marking_guidance: Credit the judgement: B, with the reasons drawn from the speech’s features and their effect on the hall.
Credit the case against A with its evidence: no address, no voice, a form that could be anything — however, note its plain purpose if the answer sees it.
The strongest answers name the test: A could open any text; B could only open a speech.

objective_titles: Write 150–200 words whose vocabulary, style and structure fit the form, purpose and audience set

items.prompt: A learner’s 200-word speech never addresses the hall and never signposts where it is going. What convention damage has been done, and why does it cost the task marks?
items.canonical_answer: The error is leaving out the form’s conventions: a speech with no address to its audience and no signposting has not shown its form, and the reader must guess it from the content — which the task asked the writer to demonstrate. The convention damage costs the writing marks because the fit to form is part of the fit to the task: the greeting finds the hall, the signposting keeps the listeners, and a speech that does neither is an essay read aloud.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the speech’s conventions, address and signposting, left out.
Must say why it costs marks: the form is part of the task, so a reader forced to guess the form is reading a poorer fit.

items.prompt: A learner writes 320 words for a task set at 150–200, "because there was so much good material in the source". Why does the extra material not help, and what is the judgement on length?
items.canonical_answer: The extra material does not help because the range is part of the task: an answer well outside 150–200 words is a poorer fit to the form and purpose, whatever the quality of what it carries — the task asked for selection as well as reshaping, and 320 words shows the selection never happened. The judgement on length is fit, not a penalty per word: no fixed sum is deducted, but a response that has sprawled past its form (or withered under it) has missed one of the task’s own requirements.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: writing far outside the range, when the range is part of the task and selection was being tested.
Must state the judgement: length is judged as fit to form and purpose, not as a word-by-word penalty.

items.prompt: Define the comparison task, and state its marks.
items.canonical_answer: The comparison sets your own directed response beside the source, opens with the instruction Compare, and analyses form, structure and language across both. It is worth fifteen marks — five for the comparative reading of both texts, ten for the analysis — and the analysis explains the similarities and differences by each text’s purpose, audience and context.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the source and your own response compared, on form, structure and language.
The marks — fifteen, split five for reading and ten for analysis — are part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response

items.prompt: Give the steps for planning a comparison of two texts.
items.canonical_answer: First, fix each text’s purpose, audience and form — the frame every feature is judged against. Then list the features each text carries. Then match them in pairs: the source’s opening beside the response’s, its voice beside the response’s, its sentence shapes beside the response’s. Then plan the paragraphs on the pairs, one pair per point, so both texts are in every paragraph before a sentence is written.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: frames, features, pairs, paragraphs.
The pairing is the step that makes it a comparison, so an answer without it has planned two descriptions.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response

items.prompt: Name five comparative connectives and say what each does.
items.canonical_answer: Whereas marks a difference; similarly marks a likeness; in contrast marks a sharper difference than whereas; both holds the two texts in one subject; unlike marks what one has and the other lacks. Each connective is the visible machinery of a paired point, which is why a paragraph of comparison carries at least one, and a paragraph of description carries none.
marking_guidance: Credit the five: whereas, similarly, in contrast, both, unlike, with what each does.
The features are named as machinery, so an answer that lists them without their jobs has half the card.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response

items.prompt: Pair A opens: "The forgotten hero of Keetmanshoop is a man nobody remembers." Pair B opens: "Dear Ms Angula, I am writing with real concern about the crossing on our street." Write one comparative sentence about these openings.
items.canonical_answer: Whereas Pair A opens with a paradox that teases its reader into the article — "a man nobody remembers", an invitation to find out — Pair B opens with a salutation and a stated purpose, because a letter must find its reader before it can state its case, while an article must first be chosen. (Any sentence that holds both openings in one grammar, on a connective, and explains the difference by purpose or audience meets the task.)
marking_guidance: Credit the sentence: both openings held in one sentence, because the pairing is the skill.
Credit the explanation by purpose or audience, so the comparison carries a reason, not just an observation.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response

items.prompt: A comparison gives the source nine paragraphs and the response two, in passing. What has gone wrong, and what is the habit that fixes it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is writing mostly about the source and little about the response, which abandons half the subject and half the marks — the task exists because there are two texts. The fixing habit is the paired point: no paragraph stays on one text longer than a sentence before referring across, and each point is built on a connective from the first word. The check is arithmetic: count the sentences naming each text, and the counts should be close.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: one text treated as the subject and the other as a footnote.
Must give the habit: the paired point in every paragraph, with a connective, and the countable balance it produces.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Both texts are about the dam project and both mention the cost." Why is this not comparison of the kind the task rewards, and what is the missing half?
items.canonical_answer: The learner has compared what the texts say, and the task asks how they are written: content is what the texts carry, and the comparison’s grounds are form, structure and language. The missing half is the writing: both texts mention the cost, but one arrives as a figure in a report’s findings and the other as an image in a resident’s memory — and that difference, in the words and the structure, is what the ten analysis marks are for.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: content compared, writing unanalysed.
Must show the missing half: how the shared content is written differently, which the words and structure of each show.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and compare the characteristic features of the source and of your own response

items.prompt: Why must each difference in a comparison be explained by purpose, audience or context?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that a difference without a reason is only an observation: two texts differ in a thousand ways, and the analysis is the selection of differences that mean something, which the purpose, audience or context supplies. A speech opens with a greeting because a hall must be found; an article opens with a headline because a reader must be caught — the reason is what makes the difference a decision rather than an accident, and the comparison exists to show decisions.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: the explanation turns a difference into a decision the analysis can credit.
An answer that says differences are interesting has not answered the why.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Explain each difference by what each text is for, who it addresses and the situation it comes from

items.prompt: Compare these two sentences about the same flooded bridge, written for the purpose — A is for officials, B is for friends: A: "Inspection of the northern abutment revealed structural compromise requiring closure." B: "Honestly, the bridge is worse than we thought — they’ve shut it." How does the change of audience work on the words?
items.canonical_answer: The change of audience works at every level. A’s passive ("was revealed" by implication) and Latinate vocabulary ("structural compromise") keep the officials at arm’s length and the blame diffuse, which suits a body that must act without alarming; B’s contraction and intensifier ("they’ve shut it", "worse than we thought") make it news between friends, and the passive disappears because a friend wants to know who shut the thing. The reader of A is invited to file; the reader of B is invited to gossip — the register, the grammar and the address all moved because the audience did.
marking_guidance: Must name the register change: Latinate and passive against contractions and directness.
Must trace the effect on each named reader: the official filed, the friend gossiped, because the words show who is addressed.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Explain each difference by what each text is for, who it addresses and the situation it comes from

items.prompt: Text A devotes its first paragraph to the launch day’s crowd and its last to the funding pledge. Text B, from the same source, gives the pledge in its first line and never mentions the crowd. What do these details suggest about the two texts’ purposes?
items.canonical_answer: The details suggest different purposes at work on the same content: A’s crowd-first, pledge-last arrangement holds the funding back as a climax, which suggests a piece built to be enjoyed — a feature, where the story earns the news. B’s pledge-first, crowd-absent arrangement delivers the decision before anything else, which suggests a piece built to inform — a notice or a report, where the reader’s question is answered before it is asked. The same two facts, differently weighted, imply two purposes and two audiences: the reader who chose the story, and the reader who needs the decision.
marking_guidance: Must read the arrangement as evidence: held-back pledge implies a feature’s shape; pledge-first implies a notice’s.
Must say what the details suggest: purposes of entertaining-informing against informing, and the audiences each implies.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Explain each difference by what each text is for, who it addresses and the situation it comes from

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The tone of my response is urgent, while the source is calm." No words from either text appear. What is missing, and what is the rule?
items.canonical_answer: What is missing is the proof: a named tone is a claim, and the claim stands on the words that create it — the imperative verbs and short sentences that make urgency, the long balanced clauses that make calm. The rule is that a tone is shown in the words or it stays a guess: quote them, and the tone is analysis; assert it without them, and it is a claim the reader cannot check, worth little on any level table.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the words that create the tone, missing from each text.
Must state the rule: tone is a claim proved by language, so the quotation is the tone’s evidence.

objective_titles: Explain each difference by what each text is for, who it addresses and the situation it comes from

items.prompt: What does a strong comparative paragraph contain?
items.canonical_answer: A point about one text, the paired evidence from the other, and the explanation by purpose, audience or context — three moves, in every paragraph, repeated until the analysis ends. The connective is the visible sign of the pairing: whereas, similarly, both, and the paragraph that lacks one is describing, not comparing.
marking_guidance: Credit the three parts: point, paired evidence, explanation by purpose or audience.
The pairing in every paragraph is the feature that makes it comparative, so an answer without it has described a paragraph.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write a comparison that keeps both texts in view in every paragraph

items.prompt: What is the difference between comparing throughout and placing two commentaries side by side, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: Comparing throughout holds both texts in view in each paragraph, so every point is a relation; two separate commentaries side by side describe one text and then the other, and the reader must build every relation themselves, because no sentence refers across. The test is the cover-up: hide one column of the answer, and if the visible column still makes sense on its own, it was a description — a comparative sentence, with a connective at its hinge, loses its meaning when either text is removed.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: relations in every paragraph against descriptions laid side by side.
Must give the test: cover either column; a comparison stops making sense, a commentary does not.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write a comparison that keeps both texts in view in every paragraph

items.prompt: An answer has one paragraph on the source, then one on the response, then another on the source. What is the structural error, and what is the mechanical fix?
items.canonical_answer: The structural error is discussing each text in turn without ever referring across to the other: the paragraphs alternate, but no sentence holds both, so the comparison — the relation — never happens on the page. The mechanical fix is the connective: rewrite each paragraph to open with a whereas, similarly or both, so the point starts as a pair and the evidence has to arrive from both texts. The fix is mechanical because it can be checked by search: find the connectives, or find the paragraphs that need rebuilding.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: alternating paragraphs with no sentence referring across.
Must give the fix: the connective in every paragraph, checked mechanically, because the pairing then has to happen.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Write a comparison that keeps both texts in view in every paragraph

items.prompt: Read "The school that feeds itself" (Text 01 in this topic’s practice texts). The head learner has asked you to open the assembly by telling the school what its farm achieved this year. Write the opening of the speech, addressed to the students. Write your response in 150–200 words, re-using the text’s content in your own words. [10]
items.canonical_answer:
Good morning, assembly. I have a number for you: zero. That is what our kitchen spent on vegetables this year — nothing, nada — because the three hectares behind the sports field that used to be a lawn you were punished for mowing is now a farm that feeds this school.
You did this. The ag-science class planned the rotation. The egg co-operative banked thirty-one thousand dollars — I checked the ledger myself, and I would like to meet the learners who priced a rand of profit per carton and shake their hands. The maths class does its percentages on that same ledger, and the extension office quotes our pest blog, which I mention because I wrote the first rule of that blog: never let a good observation go unpublished.
There are challenges, and I will be honest: the borehole is ageing, we lost forty birds in one December week, and the horticulture post is empty. The award money waits for a plan, and the mayor’s promise waits with it.

stimulus_text.title: The school that feeds itself
stimulus_text.body:
KATIMA SOUTH SECONDARY SCHOOL DIDN’T SET OUT TO FEED ITSELF. IT SET out to mow less grass.

That is how principal Doreen Nakuta tells it, and three years on, the joke has become the school’s proudest fact. The three hectares behind the sports field, once a stretch of lawn that cost more to cut than to water, are now a working farm: maize in the wet months, cabbages and spinach year-round, a chicken project that started with sixty birds and now counts four hundred, and a irrigation pond that collects the roof runoff from the whole classroom block.

The numbers have earned the school a provincial award, but the change Nakuta points to first is quieter. "Our kitchen used to buy vegetables from town, twice a week, and the budget for them went up every year," she says. "This year the kitchen bought nothing. Nothing. I check the ledger myself."

The ledger matters because Katima South is not a wealthy school. Forty-two per cent of its learners receive fee support, and the kitchen’s feeding scheme — one cooked meal a day for every learner — was funded by a patchwork of donors that changed annually. The farm has steadied it. The meal is now cooked from the school’s own fields, and the donors’ money has shifted from buying cabbages to buying seeds, tools and the pump that lifted the project off waiting lists.

The learners run more of the farm than visitors expect. The agricultural science class plans the rotation; a learners’ co-operative manages the egg sales to the community and banked N$31,000 last year; and the dreaded "garden duty" of the early days — a punishment roster, in effect — has become a lunchtime queue. "You can tell a project is working when it stops being a punishment," says Tobias Iipinge, seventeen, who joined for the eggs and stayed for the agronomy. "I know the nitrogen cycle now because I have seen it."

The curriculum has followed the farm. The maths department uses the egg ledger for percentage work; the business studies class does its costing unit on the seed budget; and the writing class, somewhat to its teacher’s alarm, keeps a popular blog of pest observations that has been quoted twice by the regional extension office. "We did not build a farm," Nakuta says, standing in the shade of the pond’s pump house, "we built a reason."

Challenges remain, and Nakuta lists them without being asked. The borehole is ageing; the chicken project lost forty birds to heat one December week; and the teacher who ran the horticulture rotation has retired without a replacement in post. The award money — N$50,000 — is earmarked, but not yet spent, because "we promised the donors a plan before the money moves".

At the launch of the harvest week, the school’s neighbours were invited to walk the fields, and the mayor’s representative, arriving late in a white sedan, promised the school "the municipality’s full support", which Nakuta received with a nod that has greeted every such promise since the second year. The learners, meanwhile, were selling bunches of spinach at the gate for N$5 each, and by the end of the afternoon the bunches had gone.

What happens next, nobody in the story will predict, which is how the learners have learned to like it. "The farm teaches you the weather does not read your plan," says Iipinge, picking up the day’s egg crates. "And the weather is the one teacher you cannot appeal to." He walks back up the path between the maize rows, past the classroom block, where the afternoon’s last class is studying a ledger the farm produced, and the arithmetic is real.

I write about last week’s column by a fellow Post Street resident, who blames the surge for emptying our street.

Yours faithfully,
R. Beukes

stimulus_text.title: The town that got what it wished for
stimulus_text.body:
LET ME SAY THE THING NOBODY AT THE TOURISM CONFERENCE SAID: WE ARE drowning, and the water is money.

I have lived in this town for twenty-two years. I ran the bookshop that used to be on Post Street, back when Post Street had a bookshop, a hardware store, a fishmonger and a place that fixed radios. The fishmonger is a coffee bar now. The radio man sells timeshares. The hardware store is an "artisanal marketplace", which is a word for a shop that sells the same wooden whale to people who arrived by cruise ship.

Nobody doubts the numbers, and this is the part that makes the argument hard to have. Before the harbour expansion, the town’s winter was three quiet months of wind and bond repayments. This year the winter occupancy was eighty-four per cent. The municipality’s rates revenue has doubled. There are jobs — real ones, and young people are doing them — and the bus that connects us to the city now runs twice on Sundays, which it never did when we asked for it politely for a decade.

So yes: the surge brought things. I am not the resident who wants the old town back, because the old town had a winter you could starve in, and I remember it.

But here is what the conference’s slideshow did not include. A two-bedroom house on Post Street rented, in 2019, for N$4,500 a month. The same house is on a short-let platform tonight for N$1,900 a weekend, and its long-term tenants — the nurse, the teacher at the primary school, the man who fixes the boats — have all moved out of town, because no landlord keeps a tenant at N$4,500 when tourists pay N$1,900 a night for the same rooms. The primary school has lost a teaching post this year: enrolment is down, because families with children are the families leaving.

The fishmonger did not close because nobody bought fish. He closed because his rent tripled, and the fish he was licensed to sell could not be sold at coffee-bar prices. The coffee bar, I should say, is excellent, and the young couple who run it are lovely, and they have also moved out of town, because they cannot live here either.

The town has not decided anything. That is my complaint, and it is not a small one. The harbour expanded, the cruise schedule tripled, and the short-let platforms arrived — three waves, no plan — and what we have now is the result of nobody deciding anything. The municipality has a tourism strategy, which is a document about growing tourism. It has no housing strategy, no rates plan for long-term tenants, and no answer to the question that the teacher asked at the meeting in the hall: who is this town for?

I do not think we are the first town in the world to face this, which is why I have stopped being interested in whether the surge is "good" or "bad". It is a tide. The question — the only one worth a column — is what a town does while the tide is in.

Other towns have done things. Some have capped short-lets to a fixed number of licences. Some have required that a share of new builds be long-term. Some have taxed the weekend and subsidised the winter, so that the surge pays for the season it disrupts. Every one of those decisions was unpopular with somebody, which is how you know something was actually decided.

I watched the conference end with applause for the occupancy figure, and I walked home past three short-lets and one lit window, and I thought: the town we are selling to the visitors is the town that cannot house the people who would make it worth visiting.

The tide is in. Build the sea wall, or move the village — but choose, because the water is rising either way.

stimulus_text.title: Thirty years on the 06:12
stimulus_text.body:
MY GRANDFATHER WORKED THE RAILWAYS FOR THIRTY-ONE YEARS, AND HE never once called the train by its destination. It was always "the 06:12", even after the timetable changed and it left at 06:20, because the name had stopped being a time long before and become a colleague.

He started in 1978 as a "lad porter", which meant he carried what the goods yard could not be bothered to carry, and he learned the railway the way you learn a person: by its noises first. The yard spoke in buffers and distant steam, and every wagon had a complaint. By the end of the second year he could tell a loaded wagon from an empty one in the dark, by the sound of the coupling.

"I was afraid of the engines at the start," he told me last month, at his kitchen table, with the tea he still makes too strong. "A big engine coming at you in the night, that is a lot of iron with a plan. You learn to be small and correct, and then you stop being afraid. Being correct is what the railway pays you for, and it is also how you survive."

He was made up to guard in 1984, and for twenty-six years he worked the 06:12 south and the 15:40 back, six days a week in the early years, and the journey that he can still recite is the one that made him. He married my grandmother because she took that train on Tuesdays to the market town, and the guard’s van smelled of the oranges she carried, and he has never eaten an orange since without some part of him waiting for the doors to close.

I asked him what the work actually was, and the answer was smaller and larger than I expected. "You are responsible for the train being right," he said. "The driver looks ahead. You look behind, and behind is where the people are. You check the doors, you check the brakes, you sign the book, and if anything is wrong on the line behind you, your name is the one in the book. That is not a small thing to be paid for."

He is proud of the book. Every guard kept one, and his thirty-one years of them are in a box in the wardrobe, in a script that gets looser as the decades go on. "A railway is a promise," he said. "The timetable is a promise you make to a town, and the town does not care what the weather did. Thirty-one years, I made that promise good."

He does not romanticise it, which surprised me until I understood it was the romance itself he distrusted. He saw two colleagues injured on the yard — one badly — and he kept the rule his first foreman gave him: never walk between a moving wagon and anything that is not moving. "The railway forgives nothing," he said, "and that is exactly why you can trust it. It never once surprised me in thirty-one years, because I never once gave it the chance."

He retired in 2009, on a Friday, and he rode the 06:12 one last time as a passenger, in a seat, "which was strange, because I kept standing up to check the doors." He has kept one photograph of himself on the platform at the start, twenty-one years old, in a uniform two sizes hopeful, and he says the boy in it is the only part of the railway he misses.

I asked him, finally, what he would tell that boy, and he thought about it while the tea went cold, and then he said: "I would tell him: it is a good life, if you are a person who likes being correct. And then I would tell him to learn the oranges are heavier than they look, because there is a woman on the Tuesday train, and you are going to need both hands."

stimulus_text.title: Thirty years on the 06:12
stimulus_text.body:
MY GRANDFATHER WORKED THE RAILWAYS FOR THIRTY-ONE YEARS, AND HE never once called the train by its destination. It was always "the 06:12", even after the timetable changed and it left at 06:20, because the name had stopped being a time long before and become a colleague.

He started in 1978 as a "lad porter", which meant he carried what the goods yard could not be bothered to carry, and he learned the railway the way you learn a person: by its noises first. The yard spoke in buffers and distant steam, and every wagon had a complaint. By the end of the second year he could tell a loaded wagon from an empty one in the dark, by the sound of the coupling.

"I was afraid of the engines at the start," he told me last month, at his kitchen table, with the tea he still makes too strong. "A big engine coming at you in the night, that is a lot of iron with a plan. You learn to be small and correct, and then you stop being afraid. Being correct is what the railway pays you for, and it is also how you survive."

He was made up to guard in 1984, and for twenty-six years he worked the 06:12 south and the 15:40 back, six days a week in the early years, and the journey that he can still recite is the one that made him. He married my grandmother because she took that train on Tuesdays to the market town, and the guard’s van smelled of the oranges she carried, and he has never eaten an orange since without some part of him waiting for the doors to close.

I asked him what the work actually was, and the answer was smaller and larger than I expected. "You are responsible for the train being right," he said. "The driver looks ahead. You look behind, and behind is where the people are. You check the doors, you check the brakes, you sign the book, and if anything is wrong on the line behind you, your name is the one in the book. That is not a small thing to be paid for."

He is proud of the book. Every guard kept one, and his thirty-one years of them are in a box in the wardrobe, in a script that gets looser as the decades go on. "A railway is a promise," he said. "The timetable is a promise you make to a town, and the town does not care what the weather did. Thirty-one years, I made that promise good."

He does not romanticise it, which surprised me until I understood it was the romance itself he distrusted. He saw two colleagues injured on the yard — one badly — and he kept the rule his first foreman gave him: never walk between a moving wagon and anything that is not moving. "The railway forgives nothing," he said, "and that is exactly why you can trust it. It never once surprised me in thirty-one years, because I never once gave it the chance."

He retired in 2009, on a Friday, and he rode the 06:12 one last time as a passenger, in a seat, "which was strange, because I kept standing up to check the doors." He has kept one photograph of himself on the platform at the start, twenty-one years old, in a uniform two sizes hopeful, and he says the boy in it is the only part of the railway he misses.

I asked him, finally, what he would tell that boy, and he thought about it while the tea went cold, and then he said: "I would tell him: it is a good life, if you are a person who likes being correct. And then I would tell him to learn the oranges are heavier than they look, because there is a woman on the Tuesday train, and you are going to need both hands."

REPORT: PONTOON CROSSING AT OMATIPA — INCIDENT OF THE RAINY SEASON
To: Regional Safety Officer. From: District Wardens’ Office, on the pontoon failure at Omatipa.
What happened: at approximately 12:10, during elevated river flow, the crossing pontoon — operating with thirty centimetres of water on deck, without its regular crew, who were absent at a funeral — lost tension on its guide cable for approximately three seconds. The radio reported the river passable that morning, and nobody checked. Recommendation: the crossing keeps a gauge, and the gauge outranks the radio.

stimulus_text.title: The crossing at Omatipa
stimulus_text.body:
THE RADIO HAD SAID THE RIVER WAS PASSABLE, AND THE RADIO HAD SAID it with the voice of a man reading a list, so we believed it the way you believe weather at a distance: completely, and without checking.

We were eleven on the north bank by six that morning, waiting for the pontoon that the district ran in the dry months and, in the wet ones, ran when it felt like it. The pontoon was on the south side. That was the first fact of the day, and it was Meme Kanyemba who noticed it, because Meme Kanyemba noticed everything and said half of it.

"They are not coming," she said, at half past six. "The cable is singing."

The cable was the steel rope that pulled the pontoon across, and in high water it hummed — the sound of a note that is being stretched. I had heard it before and did not like it, and it is the kind of sound you get used to the way you get used to a bad tooth, by deciding not to listen.

By eight there were twenty-two of us, and a bakkie with a family’s whole household on it, and a man named Shipanga who had crossed "a hundred times, in worse than this." He said that from the top of the bank, dry, with his hands in his pockets. The rest of us were lower down, closer to the water, because that is where the pontoon landed when it came, and there is a way of standing near a thing you are waiting for that is half hope and half hypnosis.

The water rose through the morning the way it does in that country — not a wave, but a slow, muscular shrug, the river adding a centimetre at a time to a decision it had already made. By ten it was touching the loading ramp, which it had no business doing, and by half past ten it had begun to take the ramp’s sand away from under it, one shelf at a time.

I want to be fair to Shipanga, because everyone at the inquiry was not. He went onto the pontoon at eleven, to help his brother start it — the brothers who ran it had gone to the funeral at Okaloko, which is the fact this whole day turns on — and he did start it, and the cable did hold, and the pontoon did come, walking across the water like an old man on a bad floor.

The pontoon reached us at noon with thirty centimetres of water on its deck, and at thirty centimetres you are not carrying people, you are carrying people on a raft.

Shipanga’s brother took the bakkie first, because the family had a baby, and the crossing took four minutes, and those four minutes were the quietest I have ever known twenty-two people to be. The cable sang one long note the whole way, and the baby slept, and the bakkie’s exhaust, half under water, made a noise like a kettle.

They came back empty for us, and the cable did not hold.

It did not break, either. What it did, the inquiry called "partial de-tensioning", which means it went slack for three seconds — a sound like a held breath let go — and in those three seconds the pontoon swung downstream with nineteen people on it, and the deck went under, and the water that had been thirty centimetres was suddenly at the knees of everyone standing on it.

I cannot tell the rest in order, because order is not what the water kept. A man gave me his hand and I did not take it, because I was holding a child who was not mine and had become mine. The deck came back up, and the people on it came back with it, all but two, and one of them was Shipanga’s brother.

The pontoon was repaired by August. The cable was replaced with a heavier one. The funeral was held where the brothers had gone, which is a sentence I cannot end properly, and will not try to here.

Shipanga crosses the river in the dry season now, by the pontoon, and I have seen him do it. He crosses standing up, with his hands out of his pockets, watching the cable the whole way across, like a man reading a list he wrote himself and no longer believes.

stimulus_text.body:
I HAVE HIKED WITH PEOPLE MY WHOLE LIFE. MY FATHER HIKED US AS children, my friends and I hiked the Sperrgebiet in our twenties, and when I tell you I had never done a long trail alone, I am not confessing a lack — I am explaining the size of the silence I walked into on day one of the Naukluft trail.

The plan was the ordinary one: eight days, the route the map calls the Mountain Trail, water at the marked tanks, my pack at eleven kilograms before the water. I told three people the itinerary. I checked the tanks were reported full. I did the checklist the way you do anything you have done competently a hundred times: quickly, and mostly from memory.

Here is what the silence is, so you know before you go. It is not the absence of people, because for two days I heard exactly what I always hear — wind, birds, my own breathing, which turns out to be a companion with opinions. The silence that arrives on day three is the absence of anyone to turn to when you see the thing you are seeing. I stood on the ridge above the Tsondab at sunset on day three, and the light did the thing it does in that country — went gold, then violet, then a blue I do not have a word for — and I opened my mouth to say it to somebody, and there was nobody, and the moment closed like a door. That is the deal you make walking alone. You see more, and you keep all of it.

What went wrong went wrong on day five, and it is the reason I am writing this instead of posting the photographs I meant to post. The tank at the fifth waypoint, marked full on the report I checked, was dry. Not low — dry, with cracked mud at the bottom and the smell of a thing that has been empty longer than a season. I had come down off the ridge with a litre and a half, which is a day’s walking in that heat and no more.

I am not a dramatic person, so I will tell you what I did in the order I did it. I checked the map. The next waypoint was eleven kilometres, and the one behind was fourteen. I sat for ten minutes, which is the most valuable thing I did all day, and then I turned around, because fourteen kilometres on a litre and a half, downhill and in the afternoon, is a calculation; eleven across a saddle in the midday sun was a gamble, and I had stopped gambling by then.

The walk back is the part I would not have written in the group-version of this blog, because it was not brave. It was slow, and hot, and I rationed water in sips I could hear myself counting, and I talked to myself the whole way, not for company but because the sound of a voice, even mine, keeps a mind on its task. I reached the fourth waypoint at dusk with a quarter of a litre and a new respect for the word "reported", as in "tanks reported full".

The lessons, in the order you should take them. Reports are reports; carry what you would need if the report is wrong — for me, that is now two litres beyond the calculation, always, even in the weight. Tell people where you are going, and give them a time to worry, not a date. And the silence is worth it. I have come back to the trail and I will go again, alone, with the two litres, because the moment on the ridge, the one the door closed on, is also the moment I would walk eight days for, and there is no version of it with company.

My father, when I told him all this over the phone, laughed for a long time and then said the thing he says: "Now you are a person who knows something." He is eighty. He has never hiked alone in his life. I have decided not to tell him that.

items.canonical_answer:
AUS: WHAT THE ONE-DAY VISITOR SHOULD KNOW
Welcome to Aus — one street, one fuel station, and the best-kept secret in the south. Start here.
EAT: The shop by the fuel station doesn’t look like a restaurant. It is one, and its mopane worms are famous for a reason. Cash only — there is no bank machine, and the town assumes you know.

THE BUS FROM KEETMANSHOOP DROPS YOU AT THE FUEL STATION AT AUS at eleven in the morning, and it does not drop you anywhere else, because Aus is one street long and the fuel station is the middle of it. This is the first thing to understand about the town, and I understood it, in a manner of speaking, by noon.

The second thing to understand is the wind. Everybody told me about the wild horses of the Namib, and nobody told me about the wind, which arrives from the south-west at a speed that feels personal and rearranges your plans around it. My plan had been to walk to the viewpoint. The wind’s plan was for me to lean into it at an angle and be grateful for the fence.

I had one day in Aus, because that is what the itinerary allowed, and I want to say first that one day is enough — not for the area, which would take a week — but for the town, which gives you what it has generously and at the pace of its own weather.

I ate at the little shop by the fuel station, which does not look like a restaurant from the road and is one anyway, and I ate the best mopane worms of my life, which I mention because it is a sentence I did not expect to write and I believe in giving a place its sentences. The woman who runs it asked me where I was from, and when I said Windhoek she nodded as if that explained the mopane thing, and we left it there, and it was a better conversation than many I have had in cities.

The wild horses are the reason most people stop, and I drove out to the waterhole at Garub in the afternoon, which is the right time, and I saw three of them: lean, wind-combed, standing at the water with the indifference of animals who have been photographed more than most celebrities. A visitor next to me whispered that there used to be forty. There are, I have since read, somewhere between eighty and a hundred, and they are fine, and the whispering is just what we do at waterholes.

I went up at four o’clock when the light was long, and there was nobody there, and the wind had dropped, and the crosses made their small shadows on the gravel. Whatever your politics, and mine are not the point, a graveyard from 1905 on a hill above a desert is a place that will make you stand still, and I did.

stimulus_text.title: The girl who fixed the borehole
stimulus_text.body:
EVERY INVENTOR HAS A STORY ABOUT THE MOMENT, AND TULI SHIKUary’s begins with a queue.

She was fourteen, in the settlement of Omutiya, standing in the line at the village borehole on a morning in the dry season of 2023, and the line was long because the pump was slow, and the pump was slow because the water table had fallen and the borehole’s old diesel engine worked like a tired man climbing stairs. "We were there two hours," she says now, "and I did my homework standing up, and I thought: the engine drinks more than we do."

She is seventeen, and this month she is in Windhoek, where the Polytechnic’s engineering department has just finished testing the device that grew out of that queue.

It is worth being clear about what the device is, because the word "invention" makes people imagine a machine with lights. Shikuary’s borehole monitor is a box the size of a lunch tin, bolted to the pump head, that measures the water table and the engine’s workload and does two things with the information: it tells the water committee, by SMS, when the table is falling — "so they can ration before the pump is drinking air" — and it throttles the engine to the depth, because "the engine does not need to climb stairs at the same speed when the stairs are lower."

The engineering department tested it against a control borehole for four months. The monitored borehole used 23 per cent less fuel and its pump needed no maintenance in the period; the control borehole’s pump failed twice. The department’s report, which the ministry has, calls the results "promising", which is the driest word a report can use and still be a compliment.

Tuli — everyone calls her Tuli, including the professor who tested her work — built the first version out of parts she describes with the affection of introductions: a pressure sensor from a washing machine, a microcontroller she bought with the money from selling her late father’s radio (her mother knows, and has forgiven her), and a phone older than the project. She taught herself the programming from a manual she read in the regional library, two bus rides away, because the settlement’s school had no computer access at the time.

"I want to be honest about the hard part," she says, when I ask what to tell other learners who read this. "The hard part was not the electronics. Electronics you can learn from a book, and the book is patient. The hard part was asking adults to test a thing a girl made. The first water committee said no. The second said no. The third said yes because their engine had just failed, and I have learned that hope is a renewable resource, but you have to be there when something breaks."

She has a patent application filed, with help from a Windhoek law firm that took the case without a fee, and she has orders — actual orders, with deposits — from eleven water committees across two regions. The price is N$2,400 per unit, which she arrived at by costing the parts, the bus fare to install them, and "one rand of profit, because profit is not a dirty word in Omutiya."

Her mother, Anna Shikuary, sells fat cakes at the crossroads and has opinions about all of this. "The radio I forgave in one week," she says. "The buses to Windhoek I forgive every week."

Tuli matriculates this year, and the engineering department has made it known she would be welcome. She plans to study, and to keep the business, "because the business is the part that teaches me what the engineering is for." Asked what she wants learners to take from her story, she thinks in the way that interviewers learn to wait for.

"The queue was the education," she says. "Everything I built, I built to shorten it."

stimulus_text.body:
THE SOLARIS 40 ARRIVED WITH THE KIND OF PACKAGING THAT SUGGESTS you have bought a small spaceship: moulded cardboard, a sleeve, a leaflet in four languages, and the panel itself, which folds to the size of a paperback and unfolds, with a satisfying series of clicks, into four linked leaves of matte black.

I tested it for thirty-one days, the way I test everything for this column: by living with it, not by admiring it. It went into my daypack, where I keep the things I promise to use — the good pen, the first-aid kit, the reusable cup — and, unlike most of that company, it earned its weight.

The claim on the box is "full phone charge in four hours of good sun", and I will do the reviewer’s arithmetic for you, because the box will not. In thirty-one days of Namibian autumn sun, mostly cloudless, my phone (a mid-range model, three years old, not a fast-charging one) went from twenty per cent to full in an average of four hours and forty minutes, with the panel angled at the sun and moved twice a day. Flat on a table, unattended, the same charge took six and a half hours. The box’s four hours is the best case in a month of good cases, and you should read it the way you read a car’s fuel figure.

The good — and it is genuinely good — is the portability and the reliability. At 640 grams it is the lightest panel I have tested at this output, and it survived a month in a schoolbag, a fall onto gravel at a campsite, and a rain shower in week three that the leaflet said would be survived and I did not believe. The two USB ports charge two devices, and while they share the total, my phone and a small power bank charged together in an afternoon.

The bad is the same bad that afflicts the whole category, and the Solaris 40 does not escape it: it is furniture, not a magic box. If you do not hang it, angle it, and move it, you get the six-and-a-half-hour version of this review, and I watched a fellow camper give up on a competitor’s panel entirely because he left it flat on the sand and expected enthusiasm. Solar charging is a relationship, and this panel is only its most agreeable partner yet.

The price, N$1,299 at the time of writing, is the point at which the arithmetic gets interesting, and I will give you my honest sums. A comparable panel a year ago cost N$1,900, and the Solaris 40 outperformed the one I tested then. Against mains charging it pays for itself, in a household’s sense, only if you are away from mains regularly; if you are a twice-a-year camper, buy a power bank and a sandwich. If you are off the grid one weekend in three, or if load-shedding visits you the way it visits most of us, the panel is the better tool and the price is fair.

The leaflet’s four languages, by the way, do not include the region’s most spoken, which is a choice the company should examine before the next print run.

Verdict: four stars out of five, and the star it loses is the box’s four-hour claim, not the panel. The Solaris 40 is honest hardware in a box that flatters it, and the honest version — a phone charged by lunchtime if you give it a morning — is worth the money.

stimulus_text.title: One month with the Solaris 40
stimulus_text.body:
THE SOLARIS 40 ARRIVED WITH THE KIND OF PACKAGING THAT SUGGESTS you have bought a small spaceship: moulded cardboard, a sleeve, a leaflet in four languages, and the panel itself, which folds to the size of a paperback and unfolds, with a satisfying series of clicks, into four linked leaves of matte black.

I tested it for thirty-one days, the way I test everything for this column: by living with it, not by admiring it. It went into my daypack, where I keep the things I promise to use — the good pen, the first-aid kit, the reusable cup — and, unlike most of that company, it earned its weight.

The claim on the box is "full phone charge in four hours of good sun", and I will do the reviewer’s arithmetic for you, because the box will not. In thirty-one days of Namibian autumn sun, mostly cloudless, my phone (a mid-range model, three years old, not a fast-charging one) went from twenty per cent to full in an average of four hours and forty minutes, with the panel angled at the sun and moved twice a day. Flat on a table, unattended, the same charge took six and a half hours. The box’s four hours is the best case in a month of good cases, and you should read it the way you read a car’s fuel figure.

The good — and it is genuinely good — is the portability and the reliability. At 640 grams it is the lightest panel I have tested at this output, and it survived a month in a schoolbag, a fall onto gravel at a campsite, and a rain shower in week three that the leaflet said would be survived and I did not believe. The two USB ports charge two devices, and while they share the total, my phone and a small power bank charged together in an afternoon.

The bad is the same bad that afflicts the whole category, and the Solaris 40 does not escape it: it is furniture, not a magic box. If you do not hang it, angle it, and move it, you get the six-and-a-half-hour version of this review, and I watched a fellow camper give up on a competitor’s panel entirely because he left it flat on the sand and expected enthusiasm. Solar charging is a relationship, and this panel is only its most agreeable partner yet.

The price, N$1,299 at the time of writing, is the point at which the arithmetic gets interesting, and I will give you my honest sums. A comparable panel a year ago cost N$1,900, and the Solaris 40 outperformed the one I tested then. Against mains charging it pays for itself, in a household’s sense, only if you are away from mains regularly; if you are a twice-a-year camper, buy a power bank and a sandwich. If you are off the grid one weekend in three, or if load-shedding visits you the way it visits most of us, the panel is the better tool and the price is fair.

The leaflet’s four languages, by the way, do not include the region’s most spoken, which is a choice the company should examine before the next print run.

Verdict: four stars out of five, and the star it loses is the box’s four-hour claim, not the panel. The Solaris 40 is honest hardware in a box that flatters it, and the honest version — a phone charged by lunchtime if you give it a morning — is worth the money.

stimulus_text.title: The night at the Otjiwarongo hall
stimulus_text.body:
I WAS SIXTEEN AND MY GUITAR WAS OLDER THAN MY MOTHER, AND I WAS going to play three songs at the cultural evening at the Otjiwarongo town hall, and I have never since been as frightened as I was in the hour before.

The fear was specific. I was not afraid of the audience in general — I had sung in church since I was nine, and a church teaches you that the audience is on your side. I was afraid of the moment between the introduction and the first note, which is the only silence in the world that is actually listening to you. In church the piano starts and you start with it. At the cultural evening there would be a man saying my name, and then a walk to a chair, and then a guitar being tuned by a girl who had never tuned anything in front of anyone, and then the silence.

My mother made me a dress the week before, from material she had been saving for a reason she never gave, and she ironed it twice, and she said the thing she says: "Sing to the back wall." She had said it since church. Sing to the back wall, because the back wall has paid like everybody else and it is the furthest away, and if the back wall can hear you the rest is a kindness.

The hall held two hundred, and the cultural evening was full, because the schools were on holiday and the town had nothing else on. I remember the programme in absurd detail: a marimba band from the secondary school, a poet who read for eleven minutes about the drought and got the biggest applause of the night before me, a dance troupe whose tape jammed and who danced to silence for eight seconds and did not stop — I learned more from watching them handle the silence than from anything anyone said to me that year.

My name was said. I walked to the chair. I tuned the guitar, which took a year, and the tuning was the performance’s secret friend: it gave me something to do with my hands and my eyes, and the audience forgives tuning the way it forgives a host lighting a candle — it is a thing that has to happen and everyone knows it.

Then the silence came, the listening one, and I sang to the back wall.

The first song was one I had written, which I have since stopped playing and will not pretend was good. The second was a hymn everyone in the hall knew, and in the second verse they sang the chorus with me, without being asked, the way a hall does when a hymn reaches the chorus and two hundred people decide at once not to be an audience. My mother says the dress was ruined by the tears by the end of the third song; I sang the third to the back wall with my eyes shut.

I did not win the evening’s small prize — the poet did, and rightly; eleven minutes about the drought and the biggest applause were no accident. The organiser paid me N$50 and a plate of food, and I still have the fifty somewhere, unfolded, because that was the first money anyone ever paid me to sing, and I did not know how to spend the first of a thing.

What I know now, that I did not know at the chair: the silence between the name and the first note is not the audience examining you. It is the audience arranging itself — getting ready to be with you. Two hundred people deciding at once to listen is the most generous thing a room can do, and a frightened girl in an ironed dress owes that room only one thing, which is to start.

I started. That is the whole story of my working life, told at its true size.

stimulus_text.title: The town that saved its water
stimulus_text.body:
THE TOWN OF ARANOS HAS CUT ITS WATER USE BY 38 PER CENT IN TWELVE months, and it has done so without a single fine, by reorganising itself around a simple idea: the town watches its own water, in public, every week.

The scheme, called the Water Ledger, was proposed by the municipality’s engineer, Loide Kambonde, after the second failed rainy season. It has three parts, and none of them is a new pipe.

The first part is measurement that people can see. Every school, hotel, and municipal building — and, since March, every household that volunteers — receives a weekly card with its own consumption on it, alongside the town’s total and the dam’s level. The cards are also posted at the fuel station, the clinic and the two shops. "People cannot save a number they never see," Kambonde says. "We had a tariff table nobody read. Now we have a noticeboard the whole town argues about."

The second part is the repair brigade — twelve residents, trained by the municipality and paid from the scheme’s budget, who fix leaks reported on a free line. In the first six months the brigade logged 437 repairs, and Kambonde’s figures attribute roughly a third of the total saving to them: "The town was losing water it had already paid to pump, through washers that cost fifty cents."

The third part is the tariff’s shape, which was the scheme’s hard politics. The first block of household water is cheaper than it was before the scheme; the second block is more than double the old rate. "We made the first block cheap so that nobody could say the poor were paying for the drought," says the mayor, Simeon Tjipuka, "and we made the second block expensive so that a green lawn in Aranos would cost what a green lawn in Aranos actually costs." Six complaints about the tariff reached the council in the first month; two reached it last month.

The results, at the one-year mark, are these. Town consumption is down 38 per cent against the year before, a saving the municipality puts at 61 million litres. The dam, at 41 per cent at the last reading, has fallen more slowly than the three-year average for the same rainfall. The brigade has a waiting list of residents wanting to join, and the schools’ consumption has fallen fastest of all — 44 per cent — which the head teacher of the secondary school attributes, with visible pride, to "a generation that now knows the weekly number for its own school, and treats it like a score".

The scheme is not free, and the town knows it. The budget for the year, N$420,000, pays for the brigade, the cards and a part-time administrator, and the council has agreed to fund it for a second year from the rates revenue the tariff changes have produced — the one part of the arithmetic Kambonde calls "the part that persuaded the council".

Aranos is now being visited by officials from two other regions, and Kambonde has given the same presentation eleven times, which she has stopped polishing: "The scheme is three ideas and a noticeboard. If a town cannot copy three ideas and a noticeboard, the water was never the problem."

Asked what happens if the rains fail a third year, Kambonde answers with the number she watches: "At the current rate of use, the dam reaches its critical level in nineteen months instead of eleven. That is what we bought. It is not safety. It is time, spent deliberately, and it is the most valuable thing a town in a drought can purchase."

stimulus_text.title: Market day
stimulus_text.body:
MY STALL IS THE SECOND FROM THE GATE, WHICH IS THE BEST POSITION IN the market and I will tell you why, because everyone thinks it is the first and they are wrong.

The first stall gets the people who have just arrived, who are still holding their money and their list, who have not yet remembered that this is a market and markets are for looking. The second stall gets them after they have looked at one stall, which is the correct amount of looking, and their shoulders have come down, and their money is now in the hand, and they are ready for me.

I sell second-hand clothes, sorted and mended, and I have sold them for nine years, since the year the factory closed and I discovered that the market is a machine that runs on Saturdays.

A market day has a shape, and I learned the shape the way you learn a river: by falling in. The first hour is the housewives with lists, who buy what they came for and do not chat, and you love them like rain. The second hour is the browsers, who touch everything, and you love them like weather in November — they bring the crowd, they buy nothing, and the crowd behind them buys.

By ten, the whole machine is hot. stimulus_text.title: Ride the Omuramba line
stimulus_text.body:
STEAM RETURNS TO THE OMURAMBA VALLEY

For sixty years the Omuramba line carried copper, cattle and the post up the valley and down again. It closed in 1974. In 2023, after a seven-year restoration by the Omuramba Heritage Railway Trust, the line carries passengers: eleven kilometres of working steam through the riverine country your grandparents knew, behind a locomotive older than the town hall.

THE TRAIN
The Omuramba Express is hauled by locomotive No. 7, "Naledi", built in 1936 and restored to working order by volunteers and two paid engineers who between them have given eleven years to the project. The train carries 84 passengers in five restored carriages — three closed, one open-sided for the photographers, and the restaurant car, "The Firebox", which serves a three-course valley lunch cooked on the journey.

THE JOURNEY
Departure is 09:30 from Junction Station, where parking is free and the platform tea room opens at 08:30. The train follows the old valley route through four working farms and one private reserve, crossing the Omuramba twice on the original steel bridges, restored at a cost the Trust is proud to state: N$4.2 million, raised by 2,100 individual donors, whose names are cut into the platform rail at Junction. The round trip returns by 14:30, with a ninety-minute stop at Valley End, where the engine takes water exactly as it did in 1974, and passengers may watch, photograph, and ask the crew anything, which they usually do.

WHAT YOU WILL SEE
The valley route passes through riparian forest of camelthorn and ana trees, and the reserve stretch is a game corridor: oryx, kudu and the giraffe herd that the warden swears can tell 09:30 from any other time of day. The river itself is home to heron, kingfisher and one hippo of local renown, named Dora by the crew and best photographed from the open carriage, at a safe and respectful distance which the crew will explain without being asked twice.

WHO IT IS FOR
Everyone. The closed carriages are wheelchair accessible and the open carriage is not, which is stated plainly in the interest of plain speaking; the platform at Junction has step-free access to all closed carriages, and the crew are trained to assist. Children under twelve travel at half fare, and under three free on a lap. Well-behaved dogs travel free in the open carriage, because the Trust’s constitution says the line is for the valley, and the valley includes dogs.

PRICES AND TIMES
Adults N$380, children (3–12) N$190, seniors N$300. The train runs Wednesday to Sunday, departing 09:30, returning 14:30. Private charters — weddings, school groups, and the famous "Footplate Experience", in which you drive — are booked through the Trust office.

WHY WE DID IT
The Trust is a non-profit organisation, and every fare goes to the line: to coal, to maintenance, and to the apprenticeship programme that has now trained six young valley mechanics in steam, of whom four are employed on the railway and two on the mines’ heritage equipment. The line exists because 2,100 people believed a valley deserves its own train, and it continues because every Saturday, someone like you steps onto the platform and hears Naledi’s whistle for the first time.

BOOKING
Book at Junction Station, at the fuel station kiosk in town, or on the Trust’s site. Groups of fifteen or more should book ahead. The tea room opens at 08:30, the whistle is at 09:25, and steam, as the old drivers said, waits for no one — but it does come back, which is the whole point of the Trust, and the reason the copper line lives again.

items.canonical_answer:
The source is a brochure for a restored heritage railway, written by the operator in the second and third person for visitors; my response is an email from a teacher to the railway’s manager proposing a school visit. Both texts carry the same product — the 09:30 departure, the five carriages, the water stop at Valley End, the Footplate Experience, the step-free access, the apprenticeship programme — and the comparison is between a text that sells the line to everyone and one that buys it for thirty-one.
